endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: To avoid conflict of interest, it is important that the validator of the solution is not also the developer of the solution.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: When AI systems are deployed in high risk environments like healthcare, independent quality evaluation is crucial to ensuring patient safety, efficacy, and trust in the underlying AI solution.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Establish minimum thresholds for performance or assurance criteria and review as part of deployment approval (“go/”no-go”) policies, procedures, and processes, with reviewed processes and approval thresholds reflecting measurement of GAI capabilities and risks.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Where expert adjudication is warranted, it would include adjudicators that are structurally independent from the device sponsor and, where the device incorporates a third-party model, from the developer of that model

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: When AI is utilized in health care decision-making at the point of care, that use should be disclosed and documented to limit risks to, and mitigate inequities for, both patients and physicians, and to allow each to understand how decisions impacting patient care or access to care are made.

endorsements.title: Toward Clinical Generative AI: Conceptual Framework
endorsements.quote: The expert consensus paradigm involves a panel of medical experts evaluating AI-generated diagnoses and treatment plans, whereas the cross-discipline validation paradigm cross-checks AI insights with those of professionals from different medical fields, ensuring comprehensive evaluation.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence translation in healthcare: an urgent call for evidence-informed policy frameworks
endorsements.quote: For these scenarios, independent entities without financial conflicts of interest should conduct prospective validation studies demonstrating that the specific tool-language-use case combination meets the patient comprehension standard before offering it for clinical deployment.

endorsements.title: The Cardiologist Driving Synthetic AI: The TIMA Method for Clinically Supervised Synthetic Data Generation
endorsements.quote: The guiding principle remains unchanged: each team member operates independently of the technical development, maintaining a purely clinical perspective that is not influenced by modeling or engineering goals.

endorsements.title: Integrating Generative AI Into Patient-Centered Clinical Decision Support: Viewpoint on Research and Practice Considerations
endorsements.quote: To ensure the quality and safety of GenAI-supported PC CDS, developers must rigorously evaluate and independently test processes before deployment [ 74 ].

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in traumatic stress treatment: The TRUST framework for ethical development, clinical applications, and research advancement
endorsements.quote: Predeployment strategies should include training models on diverse, representative datasets; conducting audits across demographic subgroups and trauma types to prioritize equity; implementing “jailbreaking exercises” to identify potential failures and weaknesses; and establishing independent validation processes ( Ferryman et al., 2023 ; Labkoff et al., 2024 ; Welch et al., 2026 ).

endorsements.title: An Acceptance Criteria Framework for Determining the Implementation Fit of Custom Large Language Models in Public Health Interventions
endorsements.quote: Ideally, all expert coders will have been uninvolved in the development and refinement of the custom LLM being tested.

endorsements.title: Empowering Educators to Build AI Chatbots in Health Professions Education: Tutorial on a No-Code Design Workflow
endorsements.quote: Pilot-testing should include structured review by a subject matter expert assessing content accuracy across a range of likely learner inputs.

evidence.title: Clinician-led, AI-assisted clinical software development: multi-domain verification of a deployed ePROM application
evidence.outcome: Errors found by independent clinical review versus passing automated tests of scoring matrix
evidence.effect: All 78 original automated cases passed, but independent review found 17 expected results requiring clinical or methodological correction.
evidence.quote: Although all 78 original automated cases passed, independent review found 17 expected results requiring clinical or methodological correction.
evidence.sample_unit: single application case; 78 scoring test cases, 52 usability participants (14 clinicians, 26 patients, 12 older adults), 926 author messages, 23 storage canaries

evidence.title: Blinded Radiologist and LLM-Based Evaluation of LLM-Generated Japanese Translations of Chest CT Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-as-a-judge with expert radiologist evaluation of translations
evidence.effect: LLM judges favored the LLM translation in 70%-99% of cases with near-zero agreement with radiologists (QWK -0.04 to 0.15); expert radiologist review remains important.
evidence.quote: For educational use of translated radiology reports, automated LLM-based evaluation alone is insufficient; expert radiologist review remains important.

evidence.title: Expert Appraisal of AI-Generated Recommendations in Cardiovascular Surgical Decision-Making: A Multisurgeon Study
evidence.outcome: Surgeon-rated clinical appropriateness of LLM recommendations, by surgeon experience and scenario type
evidence.effect: Mean rating 4.31 ± 0.8; 86% rated appropriate (4-5); Senior surgeons rated lower than Mid-Career (mean difference -0.27, p = 0.001); grey-zone cases lower (-0.19, p = 0.023).
evidence.quote: Ratings did not differ significantly between Early- and Mid-Career surgeons (p = 0.750), whereas Senior surgeons assigned lower scores than the Mid-Career group (mean difference − 0.27, p = 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: individual surgeon evaluations of AI recommendations (14 surgeons x 50 scenarios)

evidence.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Hospital Readmission Review: A Single-Center Blinded Evaluation and Exploratory Qualitative Analysis
evidence.outcome: Blinded physician evaluators rating AI review quality and factuality
evidence.effect: Blinded physician evaluators rated AI and physician reviews similarly on quality; no AI hallucinations were identified during factuality review.
evidence.quote: No AI hallucinations were identified during factuality review.
evidence.sample_unit: readmissions (each reviewed by two physicians and the AI)

evidence.title: ChatGPT as a Source for Patient Information on Patellofemoral Surgery-A Comparative Study Amongst Laymen, Doctors, and Experts
evidence.outcome: Rating of ChatGPT patient-information answers by experts versus non-experts
evidence.effect: Experts rated descriptive answers lower than non-experts (29.3 ± 5.8 vs 35.3 ± 5.7), especially for more complex questions, a gap non-experts may not recognize.
evidence.quote: The average score for experts was 29.3 ± 5.8, whereas non-experts averaged 35.3 ± 5.7.
evidence.sample_unit: raters (4 experts, 7 non-orthopedic doctors, 6 laymen) rating 12 ChatGPT answers

evidence.title: Strategic Governance of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Algorithm Development: Formative Evaluation of the Semiautomatic Clinical Algorithm Development Framework
evidence.outcome: Independent clinician review of AI-generated clinical content before deployment
evidence.effect: External pediatric emergency physician and pediatrician reviewed the algorithm; none identified critical safety errors; both rated it usable after minor revisions, pending usability testing.
evidence.quote: Neither reviewer identified critical safety errors requiring mandatory correction, providing some reassurance that execution bias did not compromise clinical safety in this single-case run.
evidence.sample_unit: algorithm development executions (single expert, single clinical topic: pediatric febrile seizures)

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-generated radiology impressions: a multi-stakeholder evaluation
evidence.outcome: Preference for AI impressions by original vs independent radiologists and oncologists
evidence.effect: Original radiologists slightly preferred their own impressions to the custom model (h = 0.18, p = 0.0716), while independent radiologists showed no preference (h = -0.03, p = 0.78). Both groups rated generic model impressions lower.
evidence.quote: Original radiologists slightly preferred their own impressions to the custom model (h = 0.18, p = 0.0716), while independent radiologists showed no preference (h = -0.03, p = 0.78).

evidence.title: Initial specialist validation of clinical decision support recommendations from a machine learning-enabled digital cognitive assessment
evidence.outcome: Independent clinical expert review of embedded clinical logic in decision support recommendations
evidence.effect: Five board-certified cognitive/behavioral neurologists rated CDS recommendations; most appropriate, with two pathways below threshold and moderate agreement (median ICC(2,k) 0.61 per patient).
evidence.quote: Five board-certified cognitive/behavioral neurologists independently rated CDS recommendations and nine predefined pathway parts for patients aged ≥55 across 21 de-identified reports.
evidence.sample_unit: de-identified patient reports rated by 5 neurologists

evidence.title: Physicians and artificial intelligence diverge in evaluating large language models on real clinical cases
evidence.effect: More than 400 physicians; AI agents were highly efficient and directionally aligned, but did not fully capture nuances and could not substitute for physician-centered evaluation.
evidence.quote: While AI agents delivered highly efficient, directionally aligned assessments, they did not fully capture the nuances of human clinical judgment and could not substitute for physician-centered evaluation.

evidence.title: AI-enabled clinical decision support in breast cancer care: a blinded multicenter benchmarking study comparing medically specialized with a general-purpose system
evidence.outcome: Independent blinded specialist evaluation of AI-generated treatment plans
evidence.effect: Board-certified breast cancer specialists from seven university centers rated outputs blinded, detecting quality differences between systems.
evidence.quote: Outputs were rated and ranked by blinded, board-certified breast cancer specialists from seven university breast cancer centers for safety, guideline adherence, medical adequacy, completeness, overall quality, and logical coherence.

evidence.title: [Efficacy and safety of artificial intelligence-based large language models for decision making support in herniology: evaluation by experts and general surgeons]
evidence.outcome: Expert versus non-expert ratings of ChatGPT recommendation quality
evidence.effect: Experts scored ChatGPT responses lower than non-experts: 2 (1-2) vs. 2 (2-3), p<0.001.
evidence.quote: Experts scored the quality of ChatGPT responses lower than non-experts (2 (1-2) vs. 2 (2-3), p<0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: questions (5 ChatGPT responses rated by experts and surgeons)

evidence.title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
evidence.outcome: Dependence of LLM-judged safety effect on judge choice; judge specificity against blinded clinicians
evidence.effect: Sonnet judge nearly halved the effect (+13.1 points); primary judge had sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.55 versus blinded clinicians.
evidence.quote: Blinded clinicians characterized the primary judge as a high-sensitivity (1.00), low-specificity (0.55) screen, not a calibrated rate.
evidence.sample_unit: paired model-response cells (4 models x common panel of questions, standard vs wrapper prompt)

commentary.bottom_line: Ten studies, nine of them offline rater studies, suggest that independent clinical reviewers find errors and quality differences that developers, automated tests, and AI judges miss. No study measured whether independent review before deployment reduces patient harm.

perspectives.view: One real-deployment study and nine offline rater studies point the same way. Most studies rated between 12 and 200 cases, answers, or reports, and one reviewed a single clinical topic. Outcomes are rater judgments rather than patient events, and no study compares tools approved with and without independent review. Limits in design and directness suggest very low certainty.

In a deployed scoring tool, all 78 automated test cases passed, yet independent clinical review found 17 expected results that needed correction. LLM judges showed near-zero agreement with radiologists (QWK -0.04 to 0.15), and one judge had specificity of 0.55 against blinded clinicians. Automated or AI checks used in place of clinical reviewers may leave errors in place.

Original radiologists slightly preferred their own impressions over a custom model (h = 0.18, p = 0.0716), while independent radiologists showed no preference (h = -0.03, p = 0.78). Five neurologists reached moderate agreement (median ICC 0.61). These results suggest that independence may change ratings and that a panel of reviewers may give steadier judgments than one reviewer.

Laypeople and non-orthopedic doctors rated ChatGPT patient-information answers higher than experts did (35.3 vs 29.3). A second study found a similar pattern, with experts scoring 2 (1-2) and non-experts 2 (2-3), p<0.001. Patients reading such answers may not see the gaps specialists see, which supports review of patient-facing content by clinicians with matching expertise.

In a study involving more than 400 physicians, AI agents were efficient and directionally aligned with physician evaluation, but they could not substitute for it. No study reported reviewer hours, cost, or approval delays. The staffing burden of independent review at scale therefore remains unmeasured.

A regulatory discussion paper calls for adjudicators who are structurally independent from the device sponsor and from any third-party model developer. NIST AI 600-1 ties review to go/no-go deployment thresholds. The studies tested reviewer judgment rather than these governance structures, so they do not show which independence standard works best.

One study of Japanese chest CT report translation found that LLM judges favored LLM output in 70% to 99% of cases, and the authors concluded that expert radiologist review remains important. Two studies involved older adults. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so no study tested reviewer qualifications for these groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared AI tools approved with and without independent clinical review on later errors, patient harm, or corrections after deployment. No study measured reviewer cost, time, or the degree of separation from developers that is sufficient.
commentary.underserved_note: One offline test addressed translation of radiology reports for non-English readers, and two involved older adults. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, U.S. limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on how to select reviewers with the language and literacy expertise their patients may need.
